articles.title: In 2024, Berkeley approved buying a 5,700-year-old Ohlone village site with funds largely raised by an Indigenous land trust, after a condo plan threatened the sacred land
articles.summary: In March 2024, Berkeley, California, finalized the purchase of a sacred 5,700-year-old Ohlone village site to be overseen by the Indigenous-led Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, ending a contentious legal dispute with developers.
articles.body: In March 2024, Berkeley, California, agreed to purchase a parking lot atop an ancient Ohlone village and transfer the property to Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, an Indigenous-led organisation. The $27 million settlement concluded a legal dispute between the city and property developer Ruegg & Ellsworth LLC. Of the total purchase price, the land trust contributed $25.5 million, and Berkeley's general fund provided the remaining $1.5 million.The site, situated at 1900 Fourth Street in West Berkeley, is the last undeveloped portion of the West Berkeley Ohlone Shellmound area, which was designated a landmark in 2000 by the city. According to the Associated Press, the village dates back an estimated 5,700 years, when the shell mound served as a ceremonial and burial site, made from shells, human remains, and artefacts. Its return followed years of disagreement over whether the property should be developed for housing or preserved because of its cultural significance.How the shell mound became the centre of a legal disputeEfforts to develop the property, which was formerly the Spenger’s Fish Grotto parking lot, were met with opposition from some Ohlone people for whom the site was sacred. Berkeley had blocked a streamlined permit for the proposed housing development in 2018, which prompted Ruegg & Ellsworth to sue the city. The project’s outline included 260 apartments, of which 50% were designated as affordable housing, alongside retail space and parking.The dispute over the development application brought Bay Area housing needs into direct conflict with Indigenous heritage protection, which landed Berkeley in murky waters of legal consequences. The city was ordered by an Alameda County Superior Court judge, in February 2024, to pay $2.6 million, coupled with $1.4 million in legal fees, for violating the Housing Accountability Act. Subsequently, the $27 million purchase, separate from that $4 million, enabled the property to be transferred to the land trust.Preceding the planning dispute, the site’s history goes back to before the Spanish colonisation, when it was home to an Ohlone village, and a shell mound about six metres high stood there and spanned the size of a football field. The same report adds that Spanish colonisers had displaced Ohlone people from their villages and forced them into labour at local missions. During the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Anglo settlers took over the land, levelled the shell mound and used its shells in Berkeley roadbeds.Plans for an Ohlone cultural siteThe transfer gives opportunity to the Indigenous community members to determine how the property could recognise and preserve their heritage. Sogorea Te’ Land Trust, dedicated to returning Indigenous people their land, secured its purchase funds with a $20 million contribution from the Kataly Foundation, a family foundation funded by Regan Pritzker and her husband, Chris Olin. Corrina Gould, a co-founder and director of the trust, led the Confederated Villages of Lisjan Ohlone, a group that represented seven tribes across the Bay Area and, alongside Berkeley, had also participated in the lawsuit. Gould described the outcome as significant for the Lisjan people, whose cultural connection to the site continues.Plans discussed in March 2024 envision a commemorative park, a reconstructed shell mound, and a cultural centre intended to house Indigenous artefacts. The potential exhibits include jewellery, baskets, and other objects held at the Phoebe A. Hearst Museum of Anthropology at the University of California, Berkeley. Sophie Hahn, a Berkeley council member, has also identified green space for Ohlone ceremonies and a burial site for repatriated remains from the university. However, these proposals have not yet been confirmed as completed facilities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In Missouri, a couple bought land with no road access and sought a 40-foot strip through their neighbour's property; a 2026 appeals court reversed the ruling that would have given them ownership of the road
articles.summary: A Missouri couple who bought land without road access secured a legal route through their neighbour’s property, but a dispute over who would own that road
articles.body: A Missouri couple who bought land without road access secured a legal route through their neighbour’s property, but a dispute over who would own that road led to an appeal. On August 26, 2026, the Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District, reversed a ruling that would have transferred ownership of the road to the couple, Clint Bowen and Morgan Bowen. According to the court’s opinion, published by Justia in Bowen v. Roeder, the couple qualified for a private road because their property had no public road access. However, the law entitled them to a permanent easement, not ownership of the land beneath the road.Couple sought access to landlocked propertyBowen and his wife purchased a tract of landlocked real estate in St. Clair County, Missouri, in 2023, intending to build a family home there. Their property had no public road running through it or directly alongside it, leaving them without the necessary vehicle access. Dylan Roeder owned the adjoining tract immediately south of their land. A road on his property ran from the southeast corner of the couple’s property to a public road, making it a potential access route.The couple petitioned the circuit court to establish a private road under Missouri law, specifically Sections 228.340 to 228.358 of the Revised Statutes. Following a bench trial on August 21, 2024, the court found that their property lacked public road access and that the requested route was strictly necessary. On September 16, 2024, the court approved a private road 40 feet wide across part of Roeder’s existing road. The designated section measured approximately 428.24 feet long and covered about 0.39 acre, or 17,130 square feet.Lower court changed its position on ownershipThe circuit court initially ruled that the couple would own the land designated for the private road, while Roeder would retain certain rights to use it. Roeder challenged this decision, arguing that the couple should receive an easement allowing access rather than ownership of the underlying property. The court reconsidered the issue and, on October 25, 2024, amended its interlocutory judgment. It agreed that the statute was intended to provide access while limiting damage and inconvenience to the neighbouring landowner. The amended ruling therefore granted the couple a non-exclusive right of ingress and egress over the road.Court-appointed commissioners assessed the damages at $3,750 for the easement, pipe-rail fence and gate. The initial order also addressed responsibility for construction, maintenance and repairs, including the possibility of sharing those costs if Roeder retained rights to use the road. However, in its final judgment on March 10, 2025, the circuit court returned to its original position, awarding the couple fee-simple ownership of the designated strip while allowing Roeder to retain certain rights of use.Roeder challenged the final judgment, arguing that the court had incorrectly transferred ownership instead of granting an easement. He also raised concerns about the judgment’s terms and whether damages should be reassessed. The appeals court resolved the ownership issue and found it unnecessary to address the other two points raised on appeal.Appeals court explained the difference between ownership and easementThe Missouri Court of Appeals examined the state’s private-road statutes, particularly Section 228.358. The provision states that a private road established through this procedure must be a “permanent easement appurtenant”. An easement gives a person the legal right to use another person’s land for a specified purpose without transferring ownership. In this case, the permanent easement would allow the couple to reach their property while Roeder retained ownership of the land beneath the road.The court explained that an easement attached to the couple’s property would provide the required access while preserving the distinction between a right to use land and the right to own it. It also noted that the private-road statutes must be interpreted strictly because they permit an exception to the general prohibition against taking private property for private use.Although Missouri law permits private roads to be established when access is strictly necessary, the court found no statutory basis for transferring full ownership of the road to the couple.Case sent back for a permanent easementThe appeals court agreed with Roeder that the circuit court had misapplied the law by granting the couple ownership of the road. It reversed the judgment and remanded the case with instructions to enter a judgment establishing a permanent easement appurtenant, along with the other relief previously ordered. The court did not disturb the finding that the couple needed access to their property. Nor did the appeals court require the damages to be reassessed on remand, as the commissioners’ award concerned an easement and neither party had filed exceptions to it.The August 26 ruling therefore resolved the legal question of ownership without eliminating the couple’s access route. They would receive a permanent easement to reach their property, but ownership of the land beneath the road would remain with Roeder.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2015, engineers fitted sawtooth edges to blades on three large wind turbines; field measurements found noise reductions of about 1.5 decibels or more
articles.summary: Discover how engineers at LM Wind Power implemented serrated panels on wind turbine blades to significantly reduce aerodynamic noise by more than 1.5 decibels, enhancing design safety and performance.
articles.body: Wind turbine blades can generate aerodynamic noise as air moves over their surfaces; because of this, it's important to prioritise noise reduction when it comes to turbine design. In 2015, engineers at LM Wind Power tested serrated panels fitted to the blades of three wind turbines and measured how effectively they reduced noise. According to a 2016 paper published in the Journal of Physics: Conference Series, the turbines had rated capacities of 2–3 megawatts while the rotor diameters ranged from 90 to 122 metres. After wind tunnel testing, the three validation campaigns’ field measurements showed noise reductions of about 1.5 decibels or more, and the results were obtained through different serration designs on the three turbines. The research examined the panels’ performance based on the geometry, positioning, and construction and addressed the challenge of reducing turbine noise while maintaining the aerodynamic performance and structural reliability necessary for operating wind turbines.How serrated panels change airflow at the blade edge Wind turbine blades can generate aerodynamic noise as air moves over their surfaces. Because of this, it’s important to prioritise noise reduction when it comes to turbine design. Serrations were then introduced as a toothed profile along the edge, which altered the airflow around the region causing the noise. The design methodology of LM Wind Power involved determining the length and position of the teeth, their flap angle, the material used, and the method of attachment. The researchers generally targeted the final 30% of the blade span, which was the main source of the dominant noise; however, extending the serrated section beyond this region was not considered feasible. Increasing it would only result in additional loads without yielding any improvement in noise reduction. In addition, panel placement also had to account for blade curvature, lift-handling locations, and fatigue safety limits.Before the field tests, aerodynamic testing examined the effects of serrations on lift and drag, and measurements were conducted at a Reynolds number of three million. In LM Wind Power's low-speed wind tunnel in Denmark, researchers compared an unmodified airfoil with versions carrying 100 mm and 130 mm serrations. The results showed that serrations increased the lift-curve slope by approximately 2% as opposed to the unmodified airfoil. They also increased drag, with the 130 mm serrations producing 3% more drag than the 100 mm version. Increasing the flap angle towards the upper side of the airfoil reduced the additional lift.Wind tunnel measurements before full-scale validationAcoustic experiments, also run before the field tests, investigated how changes in serration geometry influenced noise levels. Tests at the Institute for Sound and Vibration Research wind tunnel examined different tooth lengths, shapes, and flap angles. Researchers also conducted experiments at the TU Delft vertical wind tunnel, where particle image velocimetry was used to investigate airflow around the modified trailing edges.The measurements showed that serration length influenced noise reduction differently across the frequency spectrum. Longer teeth generally improved noise reduction at lower frequencies; conversely, their effectiveness decreased at higher frequencies. Three-dimensional serration designs also provided better reductions compared to flat designs at lower frequencies in the reported tests.The angle of the panels was another important factor. In tests at the Institute for Sound and Vibration Research, changing the flap angle produced differences of up to 3.5 decibels at individual frequencies, separate from the overall field reductions, and demonstrated that a panel’s effectiveness was contingent on its geometry and the airflow conditions. Furthermore, the engineers also developed models to predict the aerodynamic, acoustic, and structural performance of serrations. These models were based on wind tunnel measurements, field acoustic tests, and strain-gauge measurements used to assess the bending forces acting on the panels.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Boston school custodian donated his kidney to a stranger to save his colleague’s younger brother; a year later, both men were doing well
articles.summary: A Boston school custodian’s decision to donate a kidney to a stranger helped give his colleague’s younger brother a second chance at life.
articles.body: A Boston school custodian’s decision to donate a kidney to a stranger helped give his colleague’s younger brother a second chance at life. Andrew Allen, 53, worked night shifts at Boston Arts Academy, where he became friends with geometry teacher Tom Thermidor. When Thermidor revealed that his younger brother, Thomas, was suffering from stage 5 kidney failure and needed a transplant, Allen volunteered to become a donor. Although Allen’s kidney was not a direct match for Thomas, he proceeded with the donation through a kidney-exchange programme. His kidney went to another patient, helping Thomas receive a compatible organ from an anonymous donor. More than a year after their surgeries, both men were doing well, and Allen’s extraordinary gesture earned him recognition as an unsung hero.A school custodian stepped in to help his colleague’s brotherThomas Thermidor was 21 and studying at Babson College when he began experiencing headaches and chest pains. Initially, he thought he might have Covid-19, but his condition worsened, leaving him struggling to breathe. His girlfriend urged him to seek medical attention, where blood tests revealed stage 5 kidney failure.Within three months, Thomas had started dialysis, and his family began searching for a suitable donor. His two older brothers were tested but were rejected as potential donors, leaving the family facing an increasingly difficult situation.Meanwhile, at Boston Arts Academy, his older brother, Tom Thermidor, had developed a friendship with Allen, who worked the night shift as a custodian. After noticing that his colleague seemed troubled, Allen learnt about the younger brother’s condition and the unsuccessful search for a donor.Allen went home, researched living kidney donation online and submitted an application to Massachusetts General Hospital’s Living Donor Programme that same night. He later said his Christian faith had motivated him to take the first step.Why Andrew Allen donated his kidney to a strangerMedical testing established that Allen was not a suitable direct match for Thomas. However, this did not end his effort to help his colleague’s family.Through a kidney-exchange programme, Allen agreed to donate his kidney to another patient whose body could accept it. In return, the arrangement helped Thomas receive a compatible kidney from an anonymous donor.Allen underwent surgery to donate his kidney on June 3, 2025. Thomas received his transplant on August 20, 2025, after spending months undergoing dialysis and waiting for a suitable organ.Kidney exchanges help people whose willing donors are medically incompatible with them. Instead of abandoning the possibility of a living donation, the donor can provide an organ to another patient, allowing a compatible donor to help the intended recipient.For Thomas, the arrangement offered a way forward after both his older brothers had been ruled out. Although Allen’s kidney did not go directly to him, the donation helped make his transplant possible.A year later, both men were doing wellMore than a year after the two operations, Allen and Thomas were reported to be in good health and high spirits. Their families had also developed a close bond following the experience.Thomas described Allen as a source of hope during one of the darkest periods of his life. He said he had struggled to believe that someone outside his immediate family would volunteer to undergo surgery to help him.Allen, meanwhile, was reluctant to accept individual praise for his decision. He described himself as an ordinary person and said that anyone could make a similar choice.The experience also influenced Thomas’s outlook on generosity. After graduating from Babson College in May 2026, he joined Mass General Brigham’s development and philanthropy department. He said he was grateful for the opportunity to give back to the hospital system that had helped him and hoped to carry out anonymous acts of kindness himself in the future.Boston school custodian honoured as an unsung heroBoston Arts Academy recognised Allen during a National Custodian Day event on October 2, 2026. The celebration honoured the school’s custodial staff, with Allen receiving special recognition for his kidney donation.The Boston Arts Academy Foundation organised the surprise presentation, and Allen received proclamations acknowledging his contribution from Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu and US Representative Ayanna Pressley.The ceremony brought Allen and the Thermidor family together to mark the impact of the donation. Their story also highlighted the contribution of school support staff, whose work often takes place outside the spotlight.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Then, you are not Gen Z?’ Delhi High Court’s light-hearted exchange with CJP leaders; Dipke reacts
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court had a light-hearted exchange during a hearing on Wednesday involving Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court had a light-hearted exchange during a hearing on Wednesday involving Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, with Justice Subramonium Prasad remarking that the two were not part of Generation Z after being told their ages.During the hearing, Justice Prasad asked advocate Abhik Chimni, appearing for the petitioners, how old the two leaders were. Chimni told the court that Das was 27 and Ranka was 32.“Then you are not Gen Z. What is Gen Z?” the court asked.After being informed that Generation Z generally refers to people born after 1997, the court reiterated, “Then you are not Gen Z.”The exchange took place while the high court was hearing the leaders’ challenge to an October 19 order by a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) extending their judicial custody until October 21.The exchange also drew a reaction on social media, with CJP leader Abhijit Dipke posting an image of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and writing, “The only person who qualifies as GenZ.”Court questions choice of legal remedyDuring the hearing, the court questioned why the petitioners had approached it under Article 226 of the Constitution when an alternative remedy of revision could be available to challenge the magistrate’s order.“Your second incident. You are a person who has actually broken a bond. Your remedy actually lies in revision,” the court observed.The bench also questioned whether the authorities could insist on stricter surety conditions following an alleged second breach of a peace bond.“Once you have broken peace for the second time, are the authorities not entitled to insist upon everything?” the court asked.The court further noted that a challenge to the denotification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site was pending before the Supreme Court and that the notification had not been stayed. It questioned the petitioners’ decision to return to the site in those circumstances.The bench also expressed concern that breaking barricades could encourage others to violate prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).“The two petitioners here are at the forefront. When you go and break a barricade, the chances of 10 or 20 more people in violation of 163 are very high,” the court observed.Petition withdrawnAdvocate Chimni argued that the SEM's October 19 order extending the petitioners' custody was legally unsustainable. He contended that the magistrate lacked jurisdiction to extend their custody and alleged that preventive proceedings were being used arbitrarily.He also questioned the rejection of the sureties, arguing that two additional sureties were available but had not been called for consideration.According to his submissions, the magistrate's order referred to discrepancies in photographs and difficulties in verifying details relating to one of the petitioners.The court suggested that the petitioners await the outcome of proceedings before the SEM, which was scheduled to reconsider their sureties at 2 pm on Wednesday. Chimni, however, expressed apprehension that the sureties could again be rejected on fresh grounds, requiring the petitioners to approach the High Court again.The petitioners subsequently withdrew their plea. Justice Prasad permitted the withdrawal, and the High Court clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case.Additional solicitor general Chetan Sharma, along with advocate Ashish Dixit, appeared for the Delhi Police, while Chimni represented Das, Ranka and the other petitioners.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Virginia is dismantling 100,000 tons of concrete from its $3.9 billion Hampton Roads bridge-tunnel expansion; 951 tons have already been placed underwater as part of a project to build fish habitat in Chesapeake Bay
articles.summary: A bridge built to carry thousands of vehicles across Virginia's waterways is getting a second life beneath them.
articles.body: A bridge built to carry thousands of vehicles across Virginia's waterways is getting a second life beneath them. As part of the $3.9 billion Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel expansion, crews are dismantling decades-old infrastructure and sending the concrete to artificial reefs in Chesapeake Bay, where it can provide shelter for marine life. By the time the project is completed, workers are expected to have removed around 100,000 tons of concrete, with 951 tons already delivered to Bluefish Rock Reef, according to a June report by WHRO.The initiative is intended to reduce the amount of demolition waste sent to landfills while adding structures to underwater habitats. Rather than treating the old bridge material solely as construction debris, Virginia's transportation authorities and marine-resource officials are using it to expand an artificial reef programme that has been operating for decades.From bridge rubble to underwater habitatThe Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel connects the Hampton and Norfolk areas of Virginia. Its expansion involves constructing two new tunnels and trestle bridges to double the number of driving lanes. Making room for the new infrastructure also requires the removal of older sections of the bridge system.Ryan Banas, the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel Expansion project director for the Virginia Department of Transportation, told WHRO that the material being dismantled includes bridge decks, the beams supporting them and the piles or foundations extending into the bay floor.The scale of the planned removal is substantial. WHRO reported in June that approximately 100,000 tons of concrete, equivalent to about 200 million pounds, were expected to be dismantled by the time the expansion was completed in 2027. That figure is the projected total for the project, not the amount already placed underwater.The contractor is working with the state to redirect suitable material to artificial reef sites. Banas said the approach allows the project to reuse material that might otherwise be demolished and sent to landfills, while supporting wildlife habitat. The reuse strategy may also be cheaper than conventional disposal. However, Banas said officials had not provided a precise estimate of the savings, so the financial benefit cannot yet be quantified.How the concrete reaches the seabedThe process involves more than dumping rubble into the water. According to WHRO, demolished sections are loaded onto barges and transported offshore. A large crane, using a block-and-pulley system, then lowers the concrete onto the bay floor. Individual pieces can weigh as much as 50,000 pounds. Their size and weight make careful positioning essential, particularly at sites used by boats and other vessels.Hunter Smith, an artificial reef specialist with the Virginia Marine Resources Commission (VMRC), told WHRO that three-dimensional imaging is used to help ensure the material is placed according to restrictions designed to prevent navigation hazards. The placement process must also follow the applicable requirements for each permitted reef site.The project's official materials-management plan sets out conditions for using demolition material at artificial reefs, including minimum water-depth requirements and compliance with the commission's terms. It identifies Bluefish Rock Reef among the potential receiving sites and explains that suitability depends on the conditions at each location.By June 2026, the contractor had delivered 951 tons of rubble to Bluefish Rock Reef, located approximately four miles east of Buckroe Beach in Hampton. WHRO reported that demolition had been limited at that stage, with activity expected to increase as traffic moved fully onto the new bridges.Why artificial reefs matterArtificial reefs create hard surfaces in underwater environments where marine organisms can attach themselves and grow. Microorganisms and other small organisms colonise the structures, attracting baitfish and, in turn, larger predatory species. The structures can also provide shelter from predators and currents.Smith told WHRO that this process helps support the food chain, from the smallest organisms to larger fish. Species associated with Virginia's artificial reefs include black sea bass, flounder, red drum and tautog.The reef programme predates the bridge expansion by several decades. Smith said it began in the 1960s and 1970s, when decommissioned Liberty ships from the Second World War became available for reuse. The VMRC now manages 23 artificial reefs across Chesapeake Bay and Virginia's Atlantic coast.These sites also serve recreational anglers. The commission provides online maps and a mapping application to help people locate reefs, making the structures useful for both marine habitat and fishing.Most of Virginia's artificial reefs cover approximately half a mile in diameter, according to WHRO. Building them takes time because much of the material comes from construction projects and other donations. The rate at which an individual reef remains exposed can also depend on sediment accumulating on the bay floor.A second life for ageing infrastructureThe concrete from the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel expansion is expected to remain underwater for decades once it has been positioned, according to WHRO's report. Its long-term value will depend on how the material settles and how marine organisms colonise the resulting structures.The project is not without constraints: only suitable material can be used, and placement must meet environmental and navigation requirements. The official materials-management plan outlines those conditions rather than treating all demolition waste as suitable for reef construction.For Virginia, the effort links a major transportation project with an existing marine-resource programme. The expansion will add road capacity above the water, while parts of the infrastructure it replaces will become structures beneath it.The full 100,000-ton reuse target remains a projection, but the initial deployments show how demolition material can be redirected towards a different purpose. Concrete that once supported vehicles crossing Chesapeake Bay is now being used to create underwater surfaces where marine life can find shelter and food.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nepal slope shifted 40cm over 48 days before deadly flood
articles.summary: A Himalayan mountain slope had shifted by up to 40cm over 48 days before it collapsed, triggering the devastating Aug 26 flood in Nepal’s Rasuwa district,
articles.body: A Himalayan mountain slope had shifted by up to 40cm over 48 days before it collapsed, triggering the devastating Aug 26 flood in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, a scientific assessment released on Tuesday by International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) found. The disaster killed at least 1,451 people in Nepal and left 5,745 missing, while another 43 died and 519 remained missing in China. The findings indicated that satellite monitoring could detect unstable slopes weeks before collapse, though scientists said predicting the precise timing remained difficult.The preliminary report, Understanding the Gyirong-Rasuwa Disaster of 26 August 2026, analysed Sentinel-1 satellite radar observations from July 7 to Aug 24 and recorded ground movement of up to 40cm along the satellite’s line of sight. The deformation pointed to growing instability in the rock and ice mass before its collapse.At 8.37am on Aug 26, an estimated 132 million cubic metres of rock and glacier ice broke away from the northern face of Langtang Lirung and plunged into Lhende Khola valley, sending a torrent of debris downstream. The surge reached the border corridor in approximately seven minutes, but authorities issued SMS warnings only around 9.15–9.16am — nearly 38–39 minutes after the collapse and about half an hour after the flood reached the corridor.The assessment drew on satellite imagery, seismic records, drone surveys, hydrological analysis and field investigations. Researchers identified geological weaknesses, possible damage from the 2015 Nepal earthquake, thawing permafrost, glacier changes and snow accumulation as potential contributing factors, but could not establish a single trigger.The study ruled out a conventional glacial lake outburst flood, initially suspected as the cause. Instead, a massive bedrock failure dislodged part of an overlying glacier, triggering a cascading flow of rock, ice, water and sediment through the valley.Researchers said conventional early-warning systems focused on rainfall and river levels were inadequate for detecting sudden mountain collapses capable of generating fast-moving debris floods.“This tragedy shows that some dangerous mountain slopes may exhibit measurable signs of instability before catastrophic failure,” said ICIMOD director general Pema Gyamtsho.ICIMOD scientist Qianggong Zhang said satellite-based monitoring could help identify other potentially unstable slopes for closer observation, although researchers could not reliably determine when they might collapse.The findings came two days after another major rock-ice avalanche and flood struck Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki basin on Oct 11, raising concerns about the monitoring of unstable slopes across the Himalayas.A joint scientific field investigation involving ICIMOD and Chinese researchers was scheduled to begin this week to examine the disaster site and identify other potential hazard hotspots across the Himalayan region.You use AI every day. articles.title: Monsoon's gone, El Niño isn't: Why India's weather worries are far from over
articles.summary: El Niño is putting the world on alert, and India could be among the countries facing its next major weather test.
articles.body: El Niño is putting the world on alert, and India could be among the countries facing its next major weather test. After a monsoon marked by a 13 per cent rainfall deficit, attention is shifting to whether the climate phenomenon will bring a warmer winter, disrupt rainfall patterns and add to the pressure on agriculture.From Indonesia’s raging wildfires to an unusually active Pacific hurricane season, its effects are already emerging across the globe. Now, the question is what a strengthening El Niño could mean for India in the months ahead.According to the BBC, El Niño has been strengthening for several months and is already influencing weather patterns worldwide, with Indonesia experiencing its worst wildfire season since 2015, heightened hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific and reduced monsoon rainfall in India.The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has warned that the phenomenon could intensify further towards the end of 2026 and persist into 2027, raising concerns over its potential impact on temperatures, rainfall and extreme weather events across different regions.For India, the immediate concern is whether the strengthening El Niño will compound the effects of the deficient monsoon and influence winter temperatures, rainfall and agricultural conditions in the coming months.What is El Niño and how does it affect India's weather?El Niño is a climate phenomenon characterised by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. It is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural climate pattern that influences atmospheric circulation, wind systems and rainfall distribution across the world.For India, El Niño is closely watched because it is generally associated with a higher risk of below-normal southwest monsoon rainfall.The warming of Pacific waters alters atmospheric circulation and can weaken conditions that support the Indian monsoon, increasing the possibility of prolonged dry spells and rainfall shortages.While central India received near-normal rainfall, eastern and northeastern India recorded a 26 per cent deficit, classified as an exceptional drought, while southern states received 24 per cent less rainfall than average, according to the BBC.A strengthening El Niño could contribute to warmer-than-normal conditions in parts of India, potentially increasing pressure on water resources and agriculture.The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), citing the South Asian Climate Outlook Forum, projected normal to above-normal maximum and minimum temperatures across much of South Asia during October–December 2026.Higher temperatures later in the winter could also threaten wheat yields if heat coincides with the grain-filling stage, although the impact will depend on actual weather conditions.However, conditions in January and February will depend on evolving climate patterns, including western disturbances.Global impact of El NiñoEl Niño is expected to push temperatures higher across much of the world while shifting rainfall patterns, increasing the risks of drought, wildfires and flooding in different regions.In Southeast Asia, including Indonesia, hotter and drier conditions are raising wildfire and drought risks. In contrast, parts of East Africa could experience heavier rainfall and flooding, while drought risks remain a concern in other areas.El Niño is also influencing tropical storms. The eastern Pacific has experienced heightened hurricane activity, while stronger upper-level winds over the Atlantic have suppressed hurricane development.In South America, its effects vary, with drier conditions possible in parts of the Amazon and increased rainfall and flooding in some southern areas.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Demands comprehensive federal response’: 105 US lawmakers urge FBI to probe Hindu temple shooting plot amid hate crime concerns
articles.summary: A coalition of 105 US lawmakers is calling for an FBI investigation into an alleged shooting plot at a Hindu temple in Illinois, expressing concerns over rising anti-South Asian hate. This follows the arrest of a neo-Nazi suspect linked to the incident.
articles.body: A group of 105 US lawmakers has urged the FBI to investigate an alleged shooting plot at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, as a potential federal hate crime, citing concerns about anti-Indian, anti-Hindu and broader anti-South Asian hostility.Led by Indian American Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, wrote to FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday, asking for an update on the investigation into the alleged plot at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) temple and the bureau’s efforts to address credible threats against South Asian communities.Krishnamoorthi and his family were worshipping at the temple when the alleged incident occurred on October 11.“The alleged combination of targeted racial hatred, a religious setting, and preparations for mass violence demands a comprehensive federal response,” the lawmakers wrote.The group included the entire Illinois House Democratic delegation, every Indian American member of Congress, and Senators Dick Durbin, Tammy Duckworth, Andy Kim and Chris Van Hollen.Alexandros Paporakis, 19, was arrested on October 11 in connection with the alleged plot. According to prosecutors, he attempted to shoot a man outside the temple, but his rifle jammed. He fled the scene and later communicated plans to return, prompting a co-worker to alert police, who arrested him that day.Prosecutors allege that Paporakis, who identified himself as a neo-Nazi, wrote an eight-page white supremacist manifesto describing violence against people of Indian descent at a Hindu place of worship. Investigators recovered a rifle, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, body armour and white supremacist imagery, as per the press release.The letter asks whether the FBI is examining potential racial, ethnic and religious bias in the case and whether online platforms or other individuals may have helped facilitate the alleged plot. The lawmakers also want to know whether the bureau is coordinating with the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division and the relevant US Attorney’s Office.The request comes amid concerns about online hate targeting South Asians in the US. The lawmakers cited a September 2026 report that identified more than 542,000 anti-South Asian hateful posts on X between January 2025 and June 2026. The monthly volume reportedly rose by about 240% between January 2024 and June 2026.They also cited a Carnegie Endowment survey in which 48% of Indian American respondents said they had encountered racist posts targeting their community very or somewhat often since the start of 2025. One in four respondents reported being called a slur.The letter criticised messages posted by Trump administration agencies that the lawmakers said risk reinforcing racial and religious stereotypes. Examples included a Department of Homeland Security post targeting a Sikh man with a remark about driving and a Department of Education post declaring “Make College Football Great Again” after a Texas Republican complained about South Asians attending a University of Texas football game.The lawmakers argued that political debates over immigration and public safety should not lead to collective suspicion of Indian, Sikh, Hindu or other South Asian communities.They have asked the FBI to clarify how it distinguishes protected speech, including offensive expression, from credible threats that warrant investigation. They also want details of how actionable intelligence is shared with local law enforcement and potentially targeted places of worship.Other questions concern whether the bureau has sufficient personnel, language expertise and analytical resources to assess threats involving anti-Indian, anti-Hindu and broader anti-South Asian bias.The lawmakers requested a written response by October 29, to the extent permitted by the ongoing investigation. They urged the bureau to examine all relevant evidence, pursue applicable offences and explain what steps are being taken to protect affected communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1997, just 500 hardcover copies of the first Harry Potter book were printed, most for libraries; 29 years later, one surviving first edition with the original printing errors sold for $400,000 in Dallas
articles.summary: When Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone was first published in 1997, only 500 hardcover copies were printed.
articles.body: When Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone was first published in 1997, only 500 hardcover copies were printed. Most were intended for libraries, where children could borrow and read them. Nearly three decades later, one of those early copies fetched $400,000 at auction, helped by its rarity and the printing errors preserved in its pages and cover.According to American auction house Heritage Auctions, the book sold on October 14, 2026, at its Rare Books Signature Auction in Dallas, Texas. The final price of $400,000 included the buyer’s premium. The winning bid before the premium was $320,000, making the book one of the most expensive copies of Rowling’s debut novel to sell at auction. Heritage said it achieved the second-highest auction price for the title, behind a copy that sold for $471,000 in December 2021.Why this first edition is so rareThe book was published by Bloomsbury in the UK in 1997, with cover illustrations by Thomas Taylor. Although 5,650 hardcover and paperback copies were printed for the first edition, the hardcover version was far scarcer: just 500 copies were produced in that binding. As reported by The Independent, 300 of the 500 hardcovers went to schools and libraries, while the remaining 200 were distributed to friends, reviewers and other contacts. Their original purpose was to put the story into readers’ hands, rather than to create a collectible edition.The printing errors collectors look forThe copy sold in Dallas retained the identifying features of the first printing. These include a list of school supplies on page 53 in which “1 wand” appears twice. The copyright page also gives the author’s name as “Joanne Rowling”, rather than the familiar “J.K. Rowling”. There are errors on the rear cover, too. The word “Philosopher’s” is misspelled as “Philospher’s”, missing an “o”. The book’s copyright page also has no space between “Taylor” and “1997”.These details help identify the first printing and distinguish it from later editions. In this case, the book retained the original pictorial boards and was housed in a custom clamshell case made by the Chelsea Bindery, according to Heritage Auctions. As per the official website of the auction house, the copy was in very good condition, with some rubbing at the spine ends and corners, minor scratches on the rear board and lightly browned pages. Despite these signs of age, the book remained an example of the scarce original hardcover edition.A $400,000 sale, but not the auction recordThe copy attracted strong bidding before reaching its final price. According to the New York Post, the sale followed a four-minute bidding contest. Its final price, including the buyer’s premium, was $400,000. That figure is substantial, but it did not break the auction record for the title. Heritage Auctions established the current record in December 2021, when another copy sold for $471,000.The latest sale also came as a new screen adaptation of the Harry Potter story is scheduled to arrive. articles.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has warned that the country’s troops will “mercilessly eliminate” South Korean forces if their warning fire causes actual harm to North Korean territory or soldiers, as Pyongyang prepares to reactivate anti-Seoul propaganda loudspeakers along the entire border by the end of October.In a statement carried by state media KCNA on Wednesday, the director of the general affairs department of the workers' party of Korea accused South Korean forces of issuing loudspeaker warnings and firing warning shots at North Korean troops involved in fortifying the heavily militarised border. She said North Korean forces were exercising restraint while preparing for any contingency.“If the enemy’s provocative warning fire goes beyond its stated purpose and results in actual harm to the safety of our territory or our soldiers, our border troops will mercilessly eliminate the armed thugs who have lost their reason,” Kim Yo said, as quoted by Reuters.Kim made the remarks after visiting border locations with North Korean Army Marshal Pak Jong Chon, amid rising tensions between the two Koreas over Pyongyang’s fortification work.“Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border,” she said, referring to South Korea by its official name, the Republic of Korea.The planned deployment threatens to reverse South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s efforts to ease tensions with Pyongyang. His administration halted Seoul’s propaganda broadcasts and dismantled its fixed loudspeakers last year.Tensions have intensified since North Korea began reinforcing its border in April 2024. Seoul has accused Pyongyang of sending thousands of workers to the frontier and said North Korean soldiers crossed the Military Demarcation Line around 50 times this year during fortification work.South Korea has also blamed North Korean-laid mines for explosions on September 21 that seriously injured soldiers near the border. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the blasts and rejected Seoul’s allegations over border crossings.Pak, who accompanied Kim during the inspection, accused Seoul of making “deliberate, premeditated and absurd” claims to shift blame onto the North. He urged troops to turn the border into an “impregnable fortress” and warned of an overwhelming response to South Korean provocations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Dragons’ Den investor called her packaging idea “pathetic”; Rachel Watkyn secured £60,000 for a 40% stake and built a sustainable packaging business with £10 million in annual turnover
articles.summary: Rachel Watkyn secured £60,000 from Peter Jones and Theo Paphitis on Dragons’ Den in exchange for a 40% stake in Tiny Box Company, after entering the
articles.body: Rachel Watkyn secured £60,000 from Peter Jones and Theo Paphitis on Dragons’ Den in exchange for a 40% stake in Tiny Box Company, after entering the programme with no previous experience of running a business. Founded in 2007, the company grew from her difficulty finding ethically produced packaging for her jewellery business into what she describes as the UK’s largest online gift packaging e-commerce company, with an annual turnover of £10 million. Watkyn’s journey included tough questioning in the Den, rapid growth following the television appearance and years of work to establish the sustainable packaging business.How did Watkyn turn an ethical packaging gap into a £10 million businessWatkyn founded Tiny Box Company in 2007 after struggling to find sustainable packaging for her ethical jewellery business. In an interview with the small business publication SBS, she explained that she had been unable to find suitable boxes produced ethically and was surprised by the difficulty of ordering small quantities from packaging suppliers.“I saw the gap in the market and knew that was my in,” Watkyn said in the interview. The company was established to make sustainable and ethical packaging more accessible, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. Watkyn said the idea came from her own experience as a business owner rather than from an established career in packaging. Her jewellery business required packaging that reflected its ethical approach, but the options available did not meet her requirements.The difficulty revealed an opportunity to serve other businesses facing similar problems. Tiny Box Company subsequently developed its offering around gift packaging, with sustainability and accessibility central to its original purpose.How did Watkyn secure £60,000 on Dragons’ Den for a 40% stakeWatkyn’s appearance on Dragons’ Den came about after her business partner at the time applied to the programme without telling her. According to Watkyn’s account on her official website, her partner wanted to return to his broadcasting career and saw the application as a way to secure new business partners before leaving.When the BBC contacted the business about the proposed investment, Watkyn discovered what had happened. She recalled that her partner’s advice was simple: “Blag it.”Watkyn said she entered the Den without believing the business had much chance of securing investment. She had no patents, limited trading history and no previous experience of running a business or working in the packaging industry. Nevertheless, after extensive questioning about the business model, margins and future prospects, she secured £60,000 from Peter Jones and Theo Paphitis for a 40% stake in Tiny Box Company.The pitch took place in 2008, according to Watkyn’s account. She later reflected that she had accepted the deal without fully appreciating the value of the ownership she was giving away. However, she said she would not change the decision because the experience helped demonstrate what she could achieve as an entrepreneur.How did Dragons’ Den boost Tiny Box Company’s credibilityWatkyn said the investment programme's most significant effect was the credibility it gave Tiny Box Company. Following the broadcast, the business received more website traffic and enquiries, helping it gain greater visibility among potential customers.However, she stressed that appearing on television did not remove the challenges of running a business. In her account, she explained that the company's growth accelerated more quickly than she had been prepared for, leaving her to manage expansion while learning how to operate the business at a larger scale.“For years, I paid myself a minimal salary while trying to keep up with the growth and learn fast enough not to break the business,” Watkyn wrote on her website.Her experience also changed how she viewed the investment agreement. Looking back, she said she should have conducted more research, developed greater confidence in the business's value and understood her own worth before entering the Den. Despite those reservations, she credited the experience with showing her that she could build a successful company with or without external backing.How is Tiny Box Company adapting to packaging trendsIn the SBS interview, Watkyn described Tiny Box Company as the UK's largest online gift packaging e-commerce company and said it had achieved a turnover of £10 million. She also identified competition and changing customer preferences as continuing challenges for the business.Watkyn explained that packaging demand creates opportunities, but suppliers must distinguish themselves in a competitive market. She said changing trends require the company to adapt its designs and product ranges, including its Christmas collection. At the time of the interview, she had observed a shift towards simpler designs and away from more luxurious packaging.Her plans included continuing to grow the company, introducing new processes and entering new markets to maintain its position in sustainable packaging. She also described mentoring smaller businesses as an opportunity to share her experience while learning from other entrepreneurs.What lessons did Rachel Watkyn learn about investingWatkyn's investment experience subsequently became part of her work supporting other businesses. She said that when considering an investment, she placed particular importance on the people behind a company, their drive and their ability to work together. In her view, a promising idea alone is not enough without a team capable of moving the business forward.From struggling to source ethical packaging for her jewellery business to securing investment on Dragons’ Den, Watkyn's account traces the development of Tiny Box Company from a response to a practical problem into a business reporting £10 million in annual turnover. Her own recollection also makes clear that the investment was only one stage in that development, with the responsibility for building and sustaining the company remaining with her and her team.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Avoid airing anti-national content': Govt warns TV channels against inflammatory debates and AI misuse
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of information and broadcasting on Wednesday issued an advisory to satellite TV channels, asking them to avoid live coverage of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of information and broadcasting on Wednesday issued an advisory to satellite TV channels, asking them to avoid live coverage of anti-terror operations, exercise caution while broadcasting violent visuals and refrain from airing anti-national content.In its advisory, the ministry asked channels to strictly adhere to the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994."The ministry of information & broadcasting has observed instances of non-compliance with the provisions of the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, by various private satellite television channels," the ministry said."Instances of similar news/visuals broadcast on multiple channels on similar topics were observed during the meeting of IDC. Therefore, IDC recommended that all private satellite television channels be advised to strictly adhere to the statutory provisions governing content broadcast on television. The committee also emphasised that inappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalized in telecast," it added.The guidelines cover live coverage of anti-terror operations, violent visuals, crime reporting, natural disasters, the use of authentic maps of India, communal harmony and the protection of sexual assault victims' identities.On communal harmony and debate programmes, the ministry said channels must ensure that programmes, including live debates and panel discussions, "do not promote or encourage communal or anti-national attitudes".Broadcasters have also been cautioned to exercise due care while using artificial intelligence, including generative AI, in programmes such as graphics and virtual news presentations.The ministry said AI tools "may be limited to assistive capacity" without compromising the "accuracy, authenticity, or sensitivity" of news content.The ministry further asked broadcasters to strengthen their editorial and content-review mechanisms and regularly sensitise and train personnel involved in news gathering, editing, production, transmission and telecast.The ministry said violations of these guidelines may invite action under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A US doctor left $1.2 million in retirement savings for his 36 grandchildren; seven years later, a beneficiary-form dispute has kept the money out of their hands
articles.summary: Edward Lyon spent nearly four decades as a urologist at the University of Chicago, and he wanted his retirement savings to pass to his 36 grandchildren.
articles.body: Edward Lyon spent nearly four decades as a urologist at the University of Chicago, and he wanted his retirement savings to pass to his 36 grandchildren. He died in 2019, leaving a retirement account worth $1.2 million. Seven years later, the money still has not reached them. Disagreements over a beneficiary form, a spousal waiver and the limits of a power of attorney have left the inheritance frozen, while a federal appeal continues. The case offers a warning to anyone who assumes that a will or trust will settle who receives a retirement account. Here is how it all unfolded.How Edward Lyon planned to pass his retirement savings to 36 grandchildren through separate trustsEdward and Valerie Lyon were married for 68 years and had 12 children and 36 grandchildren. In 2014, when both were in their 80s, they updated their estate plan. They named their daughter Alice as their agent for medical decisions and her husband, Dan Davies, as their agent for financial decisions. Their family trust was updated to include 36 separate trusts, one for each grandchild, to receive the retirement account after his death. The grandchildren were to receive the annual required distributions, half on their birthdays and half at Christmas, switching to monthly payments at age 60. Passing the account to the younger generation was meant to give them decades of tax-deferred growth. The estate lawyer, Pat Agnew, told The Wall Street Journal that he had instructed the family to update the beneficiary form.How a 2019 beneficiary form signed under power of attorney was rejected by TIAA, the record-keeperBy 2019, Edward was ailing and Valerie was incapacitated. Davies said he logged in to the TIAA website to double-check the beneficiary details, and the page showed the information as on file. When he telephoned, he said, the representative had no record of the update, so he completed a new form. Acting under the power of attorney, he signed to name the grandchildren as beneficiaries and to waive Valerie's spousal rights. Edward died soon afterwards. TIAA wrote to say that it could not process the 2019 form because it had not been properly signed, according to court filings. Valerie died in December 2020. In January 2022, TIAA told the family that the power of attorney had not given Davies the authority to sign the spousal waiver for her. When the family protested, TIAA suggested they contact the university.Why the university says Wisconsin annuity law voided the spousal waiver and why the family disagreesThe Lyons lived in Wisconsin, where the authority granted by a power of attorney can vary. Davies held general authority over retirement plans and specific authority to designate beneficiaries. The university argued that this was not explicit enough to cover a waiver of Valerie's rights to Edward's 403(b) account, citing a Wisconsin law on annuities that it maintained applied to employee retirement accounts. The family called that argument absurd in court filings, noting that Edward never chose the annuity option and that Valerie had already waived her annuity rights in 1998. The university dismissed the 1998 waiver as a red herring, because the plans require a fresh waiver with every beneficiary change. Agnew and another lawyer gave the university legal opinions that the documents should work as the couple intended.What the family stands to lose; decades of tax-deferred growth under inherited retirement account rulesTiming makes the stakes unusually high. Edward died in 2019, when people who inherited retirement accounts could take minimum distributions across their lifetimes, letting balances grow tax-deferred for decades. The tax law removed that stretch for most beneficiaries other than spouses who inherit in 2020 or later. Had the grandchildren, born between 1986 and 2014, been recognised as beneficiaries, they would have gained decades of compounding. If the family loses, court records indicate half of the money would go to Valerie's estate and half to Edward's trust. The grandchildren would still receive it, but they would lose those valuable tax benefits. The university says plan rules and the law bind it, while TIAA says its role was merely ministerial. Meanwhile, Davies still receives monthly statements, and the balance has climbed to $1.7 million.Why beneficiary forms override wills and trusts, and what other families have learned the hard wayFederal law generally requires employers to pay workplace retirement accounts to a surviving spouse, or to the last recorded beneficiary if the spouse has signed a waiver. In most cases, those designations override a will or trust. Other cases show the risk: one man's 401(k), worth more than $1 million, went to an ex he had split from decades earlier, because her name was on a 3×5 card, rather than to his brothers. In another case, an electrical engineer named his four children as beneficiaries of a $3 million 401(k), yet his new wife's spousal rights took precedence. A lower court dismissed the family's claims against the university and TIAA in autumn 2025, and the family has appealed to the Seventh Circuit. Alice Lyon told The Wall Street Journal, "It's his legacy, and this hits us all to the core."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: MUMBAI: With recurring technical glitches affecting the 101 emergency helpline operated through MTNL, the Mumbai Fire Brigade has introduced five alternative mobile numbers.The BMC announced the additional numbers on Wednesday. Citizens can call 9076333101, 9076333102, 9076333103, 9076333104 or 9076333105 to seek assistance during fires, building collapses, road accidents, tree falls, drowning incidents and other emergencies.The move comes amid concerns that technical faults and a shortage of manpower to carry out repairs could disrupt the 101 service, making it difficult for citizens to contact the fire brigade during emergencies.The fire brigade’s main control room receives more than 15,000 emergency calls annually. Its personnel respond not only to fires but also to building collapses, vehicle accidents, incidents involving people trapped by animals or birds, drowning cases in the sea and lakes, fallen trees and oil spills on roads.The BMC said the control room previously had no alternative to the 101 helpline. The number is also used for other telephone-related operations, which can be affected when the line remains continuously engaged during a major emergency.The additional mobile numbers are expected to provide backup communication channels and help prevent delays in emergency response.The Mumbai Fire Brigade operates 35 fire stations, 19 mini fire stations, 22 quick response vehicles and six regional command centres located at Byculla, Wadala, Marol, Borivli, Mankhurd and Vikhroli. articles.title: Alabama farmer living on retirement income secretly paid strangers’ medicine bills with $100 a month for nearly a decade; his identity emerged only after his death
articles.summary: Hody Childress, an Alabama farmer and US Air Force veteran, spent nearly a decade quietly helping people who could not afford their prescription medicines.
articles.body: Hody Childress, an Alabama farmer and US Air Force veteran, spent nearly a decade quietly helping people who could not afford their prescription medicines. Living on retirement income, Childress gave $100 every month to a local pharmacy in Geraldine, Alabama, asking the pharmacist to use the money to help struggling customers. He insisted that his identity remain a secret and did not want to know who received the assistance. His generosity continued for years, helping people facing difficult choices over the cost of essential medicines. When Childress died on January 1, 2023, aged 80, his family and the wider community learnt about his quiet acts of kindness. The revelation prompted residents to continue the work he had carried out anonymously for so long.Alabama farmer secretly paid $100 a month for strangers’ medicinesChildress began his monthly donations around 2012 after approaching Brooke Walker, the owner of Geraldine Drugs, to ask whether people in the community struggled to pay for their prescriptions. When Walker confirmed that some customers could not afford their medicines, Childress handed her a folded $100 bill and asked her to use it to help someone in need.He returned the following month with another $100 and continued the practice for almost a decade. Walker was responsible for deciding who needed the assistance, particularly customers who lacked insurance or whose coverage did not pay for their prescriptions. Childress did not ask for details about the recipients and wanted no public recognition for his contributions.He insisted that the pharmacist keep his identity secretChildress was determined to ensure that his donations remained anonymous. He reportedly instructed Walker not to reveal who was providing the money. If recipients asked where the assistance had come from, she was to tell them it was a blessing from God.His family did not know about the arrangement for years. Despite living on retirement income, Childress continued to set aside money to help others. According to accounts shared by his family, his children later estimated that he had spent more than $10,000 helping people pay for prescription medicines.His generosity was not limited to the pharmacy. His daughter, Tania Nix, recalled that he also shared produce from his farm with neighbours and helped people in the community with practical tasks.A mother struggling to afford her son’s EpiPen was among those helpedOne of the most striking examples involved a mother who could not afford an EpiPen for her son. The device, which delivers epinephrine to treat severe allergic reactions, was reportedly priced at around $600. The pharmacy's assistance helped ease the financial burden on the family.The donations also supported other customers who faced difficulties paying for their prescriptions. For some, the money helped bridge the gap between the medicine they needed and what they could afford. Walker said the assistance typically went to around two people each month.Childress did not meet the recipients or seek personal thanks. His approach allowed people to receive help without having to publicly disclose their financial difficulties or know who had paid for their medicines.His death revealed the secret he had kept for nearly a decadeAs Childress's health deteriorated, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease made it increasingly difficult for him to visit the pharmacy himself. He eventually told his daughter about the donations. After he died on January 1, 2023, Walker contacted the family, and Nix shared the story at his funeral on January 5.The revelation surprised people who had benefited from the assistance without knowing who was behind it. It also gave the community a clearer picture of how much Childress had quietly contributed to the lives of others.His family learnt that the monthly payments had continued for years, even though he had never sought recognition for them. What had begun as a private arrangement between a farmer and a pharmacist had become a story about a community member who consistently helped others without expecting anything in return.Community continued Hody Childress’s legacy through a pharmacy fundAfter the story became public, residents began contributing money to help continue the work Childress had started. Walker said the fund was being called the Hody Childress Fund, allowing the pharmacy to keep assisting customers who struggled to pay for prescription medicines.The story also encouraged people outside Geraldine to consider similar ways of helping patients in their own communities. Contributions from residents helped turn Childress's private act of generosity into a collective effort.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Police arrested 42-year-old Madan Gajanan Dalai in Jamshedpur, two months after his mother’s body was found buried in their Puri rental home kitchen.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: Police on Tuesday arrested a 42-year-old man who had been on the run since allegedly murdering his 65-year-old mother and burying her body in the kitchen of their rented house in Puri city in Aug. Police, however, are yet to unravel the motive of the crime.Accused Madan Gajanan Dalai was arrested at Jamshedpur in Jharkhand, where he had been working at a snack stall under a false identity to evade arrest, police said.The body of his mother, Annapurna Dalai (65), was recovered by Kumbharapada police on Aug 24 after they broke open a cement structure following complaints of a foul stench from house owner Rabi Narayan Sahu.The mother-son duo had been living in the rented house since March. Police suspect Dalai murdered his mother on Aug 20, concealed her body inside a cement enclosure the following day and fled the house on Aug 23.“After leaving Puri, he reportedly travelled by bus to Bhubaneswar and took a train to Raipur via Titlagarh. He subsequently travelled to Kolkata and Mumbai before reaching Jamshedpur,” Puri superintendent of police (SP) Prateek Singh said.According to police sources, the accused worked at roadside eateries in Mumbai and later went to Kolkata to meet his sister. “He subsequently moved to Jharkhand, apparently to evade arrest. Acting on our field intelligence, analysis of CCTV footage and other technical inputs, we arrested him,” the Puri SP said.Police said the circumstances leading to the alleged murder remain mysterious. During interrogation, Dalai reportedly claimed that his mother had died of natural causes and that he concealed her body afterwards. Police, however, did not buy his story and suspect that he was misleading investigators.“The motive and sequence of events leading to the crime are yet to be ascertained. articles.body: Hyderabad: Aerospace and defence player Sigma Advanced Systems Limited on Wednesday informed the bourses that it has secured US$19.7 million (around ₹174 crore) from a North American customer that caters to the NATO defence ecosystem for specialised ancillary subsystems used in 155 mm artillery ammunition.The company said the order will be executed by the second quarter of 2027, with manufacturing carried out within the Sigma ecosystem. This marks Sigma’s fifth 155 mm-related engagement since May 2026 and adds another product category to its expanding artillery ammunition portfolio, the Hyderabad-based company said.Sigma has recently also won contracts and collaborations covering filled fuzes, M107 shell bodies, advanced base-bleed shell bodies and course-correction fuze technologies. The latest order moves the company further beyond standalone component supply toward a broader role in ammunition manufacturing and engineering, it said.Sigma said the global demand for artillery ammunition has risen sharply amid the Russia-Ukraine war, prompting NATO members and allied govts to focus on replenishing inventories, increasing procurement and expanding production capacity.Programmes such as the European Union’s Act in Support of Ammunition Production and NATO initiatives to aggregate demand have increased the need for reliable suppliers across the ammunition supply chain.Sigma said ancillary subsystems and fuze integration require deeper engineering capabilities, including interface coordination, performance management, process control and quality assurance. The company expects its wider 155 mm portfolio to help it pursue adjacent opportunities, subject to qualifications, customer requirements and commercial terms.Sunil Kalidindi, CEO, Sigma Advanced Systems, said defence customers were seeking partners able to support complex manufacturing requirements at scale. articles.title: GRAP-1 invoked in Delhi-NCR: What is banned, what is allowed and which curbs start from November 1
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: From restrictions on coal-fired tandoors at eateries to curbs on diesel generator use, Delhi-NCR’s first stage of the Graded Response Action
articles.body: NEW DELHI: From restrictions on coal-fired tandoors at eateries to curbs on diesel generator use, Delhi-NCR’s first stage of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) brings a set of measures aimed at preventing air quality from worsening further.With several additional pollution-control measures announced for the coming weeks, here is what is restricted now, what remains allowed and which curbs are scheduled to take effect from November 1.The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) invoked Stage 1 of GRAP across Delhi-NCR with immediate effect on Wednesday after Delhi’s Air Quality Index (AQI) rose to 244 at 2pm on October 21, from 179 a day earlier.Forecasts by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM) indicate that air quality is likely to remain in the ‘poor’ category over the coming days, news agency PTI reported.What is banned under GRAP-1?Under Stage 1, the use of coal and firewood as fuel in tandoors at hotels, restaurants and open eateries is prohibited.The use of diesel generator sets is allowed only in emergency or essential situations, as specified under the applicable rules.The CAQM has directed agencies across the NCR to implement the measures immediately and monitor air quality closely.Agencies have also been asked to ensure that AQI levels do not deteriorate further and intensify measures if the situation worsens.What is allowed under GRAP-1?GRAP-1 does not impose a blanket ban on all vehicles, construction activity or everyday movement.The restrictions specified in the CAQM order focus on the use of coal and firewood in commercial tandoors and diesel generator sets.Vehicle-entry restrictions, parking charges and office arrangements announced by the Delhi government are separate measures under its winter pollution-control plan.Their applicability depends on the specific directions and implementation dates announced by the government.What are the four stages of GRAP?GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as air pollution worsens.Stage 1 - Poor: AQI between 201 and 300.Stage 2 - Very poor: AQI between 301 and 400.Stage 3 - Severe: AQI between 401 and 450.Stage 4 - Severe plus: AQI above 450.The measures are intended to prevent further deterioration in air quality, PTI reported.Authorities monitor pollution levels and forecasts to determine when additional restrictions are required.Which vehicle curbs will start from November 1?Delhi environment minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said the government was prepared with additional preventive measures to tackle winter pollution.From November 1, vehicles without a valid Pollution Under Control Certificate (PUCC) will be denied fuel under the “No PUCC, No Fuel” rule, PTI reported.Enforcement against end-of-life vehicles will also be strengthened.Vehicles registered outside Delhi that do not meet BS-VI emission standards will be barred from entering the city from November 1 to January 31.CNG and electric vehicles will be exempt from this restriction.These measures are part of the government’s wider winter action plan and are separate from the immediate GRAP-1 restrictions invoked by CAQM.Will office timings and parking charges change?The Delhi government has announced staggered office timings and work-from-home arrangements to reduce vehicular emissions and peak-hour congestion.Under the announced plan, 50% of employees in government and private offices will work from home, PTI reported.Municipal Corporation of Delhi offices will operate from 8.30am to 5pm, while Delhi government offices will function from 10am to 6.30pm.Parking charges at authorised parking facilities will double from November 1, with Metro parking facilities exempt. The move is intended to encourage greater use of public transport.What are the construction restrictions?The government has announced restrictions on dust-generating demolition and outdoor civil construction activities from November 1 to January 31.A complete ban on construction and demolition activities is scheduled from December 10 to January 20.These dates form part of the announced winter pollution-control plan and should not be confused with the immediate GRAP-1 order.How will Delhi monitor pollution this winter?Sirsa said nearly 30 agencies were working together under the government’s 11-point air pollution mitigation plan.Delhi plans to expand its network of Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations from 47 to 60 and deploy 334 enforcement teams to monitor pollution and ensure compliance with environmental norms, PTI reported.Long-term measures include end-to-end road carpeting to reduce road dust, promoting electric vehicles and phasing out polluting fuel-based industries in Delhi-NCR.Citing a government assessment, Sirsa said around 30% of pollution was generated within Delhi, while 60-65% came from or was influenced by surrounding areas.He called for coordinated action across the NCR, stressing that air pollution was a regional problem.Sirsa also said Delhi had gone longer than usual without GRAP restrictions this year, attributing the delay to the government’s efforts and public participation.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news.
